article.body: Physical memory is fundamentally constrained by how we describe the world. When we study a system, we cannot track every single atom, so we use coarse-graining, which means grouping tiny, complex details into simpler, broader patterns. This is like watching a crowd of people from a helicopter; you see the movement of the group, not the individual steps of each person. Our work suggests that the reliability of a memory is physically limited by the energy available to maintain it against the environment. [1]. Objective records emerge when these systems broadcast their status into their surroundings, allowing independent observers to recover the same information. Even when information is scrambled, which means it is rapidly spread out and delocalized across many parts of a system, the underlying states can still survive to form a stable, accessible record. [2]. We are now applying these lessons to chemistry. We use a stoichiometric matrix, which is a mathematical ledger that tracks the specific ratios of molecules consumed or produced in a reaction, to identify autocatalytic networks. These are chemical loops that can sustain their own activity by creating more of themselves. [3]. However, the exact conditions allowing a system to shift from static persistence to true, adaptive change remain a puzzle. We have not yet pinpointed the barrier between mere repetition and genuine, history-dependent evolution. How does a chemical loop cross the line from a simple, repeating reaction to a system that meaningfully learns from its past? Summary We studied how physical systems hold onto information. We found that reliable memory costs energy and depends on how we simplify our descriptions. We discovered that objective records are made when systems share information with their environment. We looked at chemical loops that sustain their own existence. We still do not know exactly when these loops become capable of true evolution. We continue to investigate the boundary between simple repetition and real, adaptive change. Readers can follow our ongoing progress on the Console.
article.lede: Our research maps how the physical world holds onto its history, how private information becomes a public, objective record, and the threshold conditions that might allow chemical loops to evolve.
article.lens: We are investigating the physical and chemical limits of memory by connecting theories of dissipation and energy cost with the emergence of objective, observable records and self-sustaining reaction networks.
article.title: Tracking How Physical Systems Remember and Change
